definition: Steel plates welded to the flanges of rolled beams to increase their section properties, often resulting in lower fatigue resistance.
Second-order geometric effects in structural analysis where lateral displacements induce additional moments due to the vertical loads acting through the displaced configuration.
Cracks that form in a concrete topping slab due to the movement or joints in the underlying precast concrete substrate.
A beam with a cross-section that varies along its length, often designed to optimize material usage in regions of differing moment demands.
The calculated stress in a structural member at a specific location, excluding localized stress concentrations such as those at welds.
A dimensionless value (Z) quantifying the influence of horizontal curvature on the behavior of a girder's web, calculated as a function of the web depth, radius of curvature, and web thickness.
A measure of a structural element's resistance to bending, expressed as the product of the modulus of elasticity (E) and the moment of inertia (I).

Internal stresses that remain in a material after the original cause of the stresses, such as welding or manufacturing processes, has been removed, requiring equilibrium between tensile and compressive regions within the cross section.
The internal stress induced in a structural member due to bending moments, calculated as the bending moment divided by the section modulus.
A localized buckling or crushing failure of the web of a steel girder under concentrated compressive loads.
Projecting structural extensions from a box girder that support the roadway or deck beyond the main box section.
Polymer-based sheets, grids, or fabrics used in soil structures to enhance stability through friction and tensile resistance, often layered with backfill.
A small, intentionally left unwelded gap at the corner of the floorbeam (FB) tooth in the rib-to-deck connection (RDF), used to avoid crossing welds.
A pair of standardized axle loads used in bridge design, positioned to maximize structural effects while adhering to transverse placement constraints.
An I-shaped cross-section of a structural member that is symmetric about both its major and minor axes.
Materials, such as horizontal strips, grids, or geosynthetics, incorporated into soil or backfill to improve its strength and stability by resisting tensile forces.
An empirical or theoretical model describing how seismic wave amplitude decreases with distance from the earthquake source.
The maximum allowable force that a slip-critical bolted connection can withstand before slipping occurs under service or factored loads.
A reinforced concrete diaphragm where shear deformation governs behavior, requiring the use of a lower force reduction factor (Rs) due to limited ductility.
Steel bars placed parallel to the axis of a column to resist axial loads and bending moments.
A type of building foundation that transfers structural loads to the earth at a relatively shallow depth, close to the ground surface.
A set of requirements outlined in the AASHTO/AWS D1.5 Bridge Welding Code to ensure the integrity and toughness of fracture critical members.
The horizontal structural element of a bridge substructure that connects and distributes loads from the superstructure to the supporting piles or columns.
Demand-Capacity Ratios used to evaluate whether the computed earthquake-induced stresses in a gravity dam exceed the allowable tensile or compressive capacity of the concrete.
Reinforced concrete walls connected by beams or slabs at regular intervals, working together to resist lateral loads.
A bridge erection method where the fully or partially assembled superstructure is incrementally pushed or pulled longitudinally across permanent supports using hydraulic jacks and roller systems.
A structural design technique that decouples a building from ground motion during an earthquake by using flexible pads or bearings to absorb seismic energy.
Structural elements attached along the length of a girder's web to increase its resistance to buckling under compressive or bending stresses.
Structural components in bridge systems that connect adjacent girders to provide lateral stability and distribute loads.

A modifier applied in buckling calculations to account for the beneficial effects of non-uniform moment distributions along a beam's length, often conservatively assumed as 1.0 in simplified analyses.
A calculated property representing the effective cross-sectional area of a structural element that resists shear deformation.
Reinforced concrete walls designed with enhanced ductility and toughness to withstand seismic forces in high-seismicity regions.
Components of fire protection sprinkler systems, specifically the vertical or angled piping segments connecting the main supply line to individual sprinkler heads.
The maximum shear force a web plate can withstand before undergoing buckling due to shear stresses.
A seismic event used as the basis for structural design, corresponding to a specified probability of exceedance or return period.
The increase in seismic wave amplitude and shaking intensity at a specific location due to local geological conditions, such as soil type and depth.
A post-buckling shear resistance mechanism in web plates where diagonal tensile stresses develop after shear buckling occurs.
The resistance of a building story to lateral deformation, quantified as the ratio of applied lateral force to resulting displacement.
A long-term, constant load acting on a structure, such as the self-weight of member components.
A time-dependent structural analysis technique that simulates the response of a system to dynamic loads, incorporating nonlinear material behavior and large deformations.
The location within a cross-section where the stress distribution transitions from compression to tension under plastic conditions, determining the balance of axial and flexural resistance.
A dynamic analysis method that evaluates a structure's response to seismic loads by combining its natural vibration modes with a ground motion spectrum.
A progressive and localized structural damage that occurs in steel bridges when subjected to cyclic loading, leading to crack initiation and growth over time.
A method for combining seismic loads applied in two orthogonal directions, where 100% of the load in one direction and 30% of the load in the perpendicular direction are considered together.
A temporary support system using cables attached to the top of girders to counteract cantilever moments and control deflections during bridge launching.
The maximum allowable duration a diver can spend at a given depth without requiring decompression stops during ascent to avoid decompression sickness.
A multiplier applied to account for the reduced strength or stability of structural elements due to their slenderness.
The localized pool of molten metal formed during welding that solidifies to create the weld joint.
A strategically weakened portion of a beam designed to concentrate inelastic deformation and energy dissipation during seismic events, enhancing structural ductility.
The pressure exerted by a fluid at equilibrium due to the force of gravity, which can increase in soil or structures when drainage systems are blocked.
A classification assigned to structures based on their occupancy, use, and the consequences of failure, influencing seismic design and performance requirements.
The distance from the center of a hole to the nearest edge of a structural member, such as a girder.
A structural system designed to decouple a superstructure from ground motion during lateral loads, such as earthquakes, by allowing significant displacement at the base.
A computational procedure that evaluates the interaction between a structure and the surrounding soil under seismic loading, accounting for soil flexibility and inertial effects.
The process by which a metal becomes stronger and harder as it is plastically deformed, increasing its resistance to further deformation.
The ratio of the mass (or weight) of a secondary component to the mass (or weight) of the primary supporting structure, used in seismic analysis.
Horizontal structural elements, such as floors or roofs, that distribute lateral forces to vertical resisting elements in a building during seismic events.
A structural system or connection detail in precast concrete elements designed to accommodate movement, such as drift, without damage.
The shear force in a structural section, adjusted by load factors to account for uncertainties in loading and material properties.
A transformed structural section used for stress calculations under transient loads, where the concrete deck is adjusted using the modular ratio (n) to act compositely with the steel section.
A table categorizing connections to be made on-site, detailing the quantity, size, and type of bolts required for each connection.
A continuous and thorough observation process conducted by a qualified inspector to ensure compliance with design and construction requirements for critical structural elements.
A structural wall in a bridge that retains the fill material supporting the roadway and spans between the bridge's arch and deck.
Analytical techniques that compare the seismic capacity of a structure to the seismic demand imposed by an earthquake, often used to evaluate performance and retrofit needs.
A seismic design principle requiring columns to be stronger than beams to ensure inelastic deformation occurs in beams rather than columns, preventing catastrophic collapse.
Partial joint penetration, a type of weld where the weld metal does not fully extend through the thickness of the joint, leaving an unfused zone at the root.
A temporary structural extension attached to the leading end of girders during launching to reduce cantilever length and minimize forces on the girders.
A noncontinuous weld composed of a series of short welds separated by spaces of equal length.
The moment of inertia of a composite section calculated by transforming the steel reinforcement into an equivalent concrete area using the modular ratio.
An imaginary line running through the length of the weld, used to describe its orientation in space.
The average length of time between occurrences of a specific wind velocity or load event, used to characterize the likelihood of such events in design.
The ability of a structural connection or system to undergo significant inelastic deformation without loss of strength, typically required to absorb seismic energy.
The tendency of a structure, such as a footing, to rotate and lose stability due to moments caused by lateral or eccentric loads.
The determination of the live load carrying capacity of a bridge using as-built bridge plans and field inspection data.
Components used in composite construction to transfer shear forces between the concrete deck and steel girder, ensuring combined structural action.
The restriction of vehicle weight limits on a bridge that cannot safely carry statutory loads based on a load-rating evaluation.
Cantilever retaining walls designed to resist lateral soil pressure from backfill and sometimes additional tractive forces at the top.
Flexible bridge bearings made of layers of elastomer (rubber) and steel that accommodate movement and rotation through deformation.
Individual layers of backfill material that are placed and compacted sequentially during the construction of a mechanically stabilized earth structure.
A seismic response modification factor used to reduce design loads by accounting for a structure's ductility and energy dissipation capacity.
A cyclic environmental condition involving alternating freezing and thawing temperatures, used to evaluate material resistance to thermal stress.
The equivalent viscous damping of an isolation system component, calculated from its energy dissipation characteristics in the force-displacement loop.
A structural concrete topping slab designed to resist in-plane earthquake forces independently, without relying on composite action with the underlying precast concrete elements.
The ability of steel to increase its hardness and tensile strength through rapid cooling (quenching) after heating.
A method of beam analysis that accounts for both bending and shear deformations to determine equivalent section properties.
The vertical alignment or lack of tilt in the web of a steel I-girder, critical for structural stability during bridge construction.
A bolted connection in a steel girder where two separate sections are joined together during construction in the field.
A form of concrete where internal stresses are introduced to counteract tensile stresses that will occur due to applied loads, enhancing structural performance.
Structural systems in a building designed to resist lateral forces, such as those from earthquakes, using diagonal braces arranged in a specific configuration.
The percentage of energy dissipated per cycle of vibration in a soil due to internal friction and other mechanisms, expressed as a fraction of critical damping.
Materials that meet specific toughness requirements, allowing them to undergo significant deformation without failure under stress.
Equivalent Lateral Force procedure, a simplified seismic design method that approximates earthquake forces as static lateral loads applied to a structure.
Structural steel products formed by passing heated steel through rollers to achieve specific cross-sectional profiles, such as I-beams or angles.
The phenomenon where a material, such as concrete, expands or contracts laterally when subjected to axial stress, potentially inducing orthogonal stresses in adjacent structural elements.
The behavior of soil layers during strong shaking where stiffness and damping properties change with strain level, affecting ground motion propagation.
Classifications that determine the level of seismic resistance required for buildings based on ground motion, occupancy, and desired performance.
The erosion or removal of sediment, soil, or rock from around bridge foundations or substructures due to water flow, which can undermine structural stability.
The capacity of a structural member to resist forces that cause internal sliding or failure along a plane parallel to the applied load.
A detailed drawing that specifies the location, orientation, and special field requirements of all shipping assemblies for the erector during construction.
Adjusted Collapse Margin Ratio, a metric used to evaluate the collapse safety of a structure by comparing its median collapse intensity to the maximum considered earthquake intensity.
The calculated bending strength of a structural flange or member, accounting for material and geometric properties under design loads.
The calculated capacity of a bolted connection to resist bearing failure at a bolt hole under applied loads.
Shielded Metal Arc Welding electrodes, which are consumable rods used in arc welding that have a flux coating to protect the weld area.
A mechanism for selecting the target seismic performance level of a diaphragm, specifying its allowable elastic or inelastic behavior under earthquake excitation.
Second-order effects in structural frames caused by the interaction of axial loads and lateral displacements, which can lead to instability if not controlled.
Horizontal structural members in bridge substructures that support the bridge deck and transfer loads to the columns or piers.
The most severe earthquake ground motion considered in structural design, typically representing a low-probability, high-intensity event.
The uniform torsional shear stress distribution in a structural member caused by twisting moments, without warping effects.
A standard design live load model for highway bridges, representing a combination of truck and lane loads as specified by AASHTO.
The speed at which shear waves propagate through soil or rock, used to characterize site conditions and modify seismic response parameters.
Vertical downward movement or sinking of the ground surface due to soil consolidation or deformation, often caused by seismic activity.
Diaphragm components that gather and transfer lateral forces from the diaphragm to vertical seismic force-resisting elements.
The required seismic design forces or accelerations at specific vibration periods, typically derived from earthquake ground motion spectra.
A specified level of ground motion intensity used as the basis for designing structures to meet performance objectives during seismic events.
A structural system of braces installed at the top flange of a beam or girder to resist lateral forces and reduce lateral deflection.
A condition in structural design where the structure's capacity is evaluated against maximum loads to ensure it does not fail under extreme conditions.
Assemblies of closed or continuously bent reinforcing bars, including hoops and crossties, used to confine concrete and provide lateral support in structural members.
A building construction method where floor and roof framing rests on non-continuous load-bearing walls at each story level.
Categorizations of soil or rock conditions at a location that influence how ground motions are amplified or attenuated during an earthquake.
Architectural, mechanical, and electrical elements in buildings that are not part of the primary structural system but must be designed to resist seismic forces.
A continuous route through a structural system that transfers applied loads to the foundation or other supporting elements.
Maximum Considered Earthquake Geometric Mean, a specific type of ground motion measure used in seismic hazard analysis.
Structural elements designed to span between foundation elements, carrying vertical loads and moments, shear, and potentially torsion from the superstructure.
A specific type of live load used in bridge design to assess the effects of repeated loading cycles that may lead to fatigue failure over time.
A groove weld where the weld metal fully penetrates the joint thickness, providing full strength across the connection.
The junction between the base metal and the weld material, often a critical location for fatigue crack initiation.
A structure, other than a building, that is designed to resist seismic forces, often supported by a primary structure and treated separately in seismic design.
Closed or U-shaped loops of reinforcement used to provide transverse steel in beams, enhancing shear resistance and confinement.
A shallow foundation type that distributes structural loads over a wider area of soil, used when bearing capacity is sufficient.
A structural element used in bridge construction, typically hollow and rectangular or trapezoidal in cross-section, designed to carry loads efficiently over long spans.
Maximum Design Flood, an extreme flood condition with an unlimited return period used to evaluate the worst structural loading scenario for floodwalls.

Classifications of precast concrete diaphragm connectors or joint reinforcements based on their ability to undergo controlled deformation, categorized as Low, Moderate, or High Deformability Elements.
Steel beam sections with a web that is thin relative to its height, making them more susceptible to buckling and requiring specific design checks.
A structural partition or barrier within a box section or orthotropic steel deck (OSD) panel that provides rigidity and alignment during fabrication.
A structural feature, such as post-tensioning, that enables a building or wall to return to its original position after experiencing lateral displacement due to seismic forces.
A method of analyzing bridge girders as individual beams, incorporating composite action between the beam and deck and using live load distribution factors from design codes.
Conditions beyond which a bridge or structural component no longer satisfies the design requirements for safety or serviceability.
A material property representing the stiffness of a material, defined as the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic region of deformation.

A computational method used to determine the critical load at which a structural element will buckle, based on solving an eigenvalue problem derived from the system's stiffness and geometric matrices.
Parameters used in seismic design codes to adjust ground motion estimates based on local soil or geological conditions.
A specific design load scenario used to evaluate the fatigue life of structural details under repeated live loads.
Metal connectors welded to the top flange of a steel beam to transfer shear forces between the beam and the concrete slab, enabling composite action.
The modification of seismic waves as they travel through near-surface geological layers, affecting ground motion characteristics at a specific location.
A curve representing the combination of axial force and bending moment at which initial yielding occurs in a structural member's cross-section.
Abutment structures that are rigidly connected to the bridge deck, eliminating expansion joints and allowing the superstructure and substructure to act as a single unit.

The ability of a reinforced concrete diaphragm or structural element to undergo significant inelastic deformation without substantial loss of strength, often quantified as a ratio of ultimate to yield displacement.
A failure mode in structural steel where a tension member breaks along a line through holes or other discontinuities, reducing its effective cross-sectional area.
A representative seismic event on a fault, typically the largest magnitude earthquake considered likely to occur based on fault-specific geological data.
A bending condition in a structural section where the top flange is in tension and the bottom flange is in compression.
A steel manufacturing process that uses a significant proportion of recycled scrap metal as the primary raw material instead of iron ore.
High-load multi-rotational bearings, a type of bridge bearing assembly that includes elements like pots, discs, and concave/convex plates designed for high load capacity and rotational movement.
The amplitude of cyclic shear strain in a soil element, used to characterize the level of deformation influencing stiffness and damping properties.
Geospatial representations that quantify the probability and severity of earthquake ground motions in a given region for engineering design purposes.
Deformed reinforcing bars with mechanically attached heads at one or both ends to enhance anchorage and load transfer within concrete.
A point along a continuous span where the bending moment changes sign, used as a reference for determining girder depth optimization.
Earth or other material used to fill an excavation behind a structure, such as a retaining wall or abutment, often compacted in layers to provide stability.
A steel plate used to connect diagonal cross-frame members to the girder, transferring forces between components.
The part of a building's structural system that provides resistance to horizontal forces acting on the structure.
The design earthquake ground motion level used as a basis for evaluating the performance of structural and nonstructural components under seismic loading.
Structural components designed to withstand and dissipate seismic forces during an earthquake.
Abrupt changes in the geometry or stiffness of reinforced concrete walls between stories, often leading to stress concentrations and potential earthquake damage.
The secant stiffness of an isolation system component derived from its force-displacement relationship, accounting for its nonlinear behavior under lateral loads.
A refined structural analysis method that models all components of a bridge superstructure in three dimensions to accurately distribute loads based on actual stiffness.
Intentional grooves or cuts made in a concrete topping slab to control the location of cracking caused by underlying precast concrete joints or shrinkage.
A factor used in seismic design to account for the reliability of the structural system, where a value of 1.0 indicates no additional penalty for lack of redundancy.

Phased-array ultrasonic testing, an advanced form of ultrasonic testing that uses multiple ultrasonic elements and electronic time delays to steer, focus, and scan beams for enhanced inspection of welds and materials.
A closed-section steel structural element used in bridge construction, characterized by a box-like shape that provides high torsional resistance and aesthetic advantages.
Loads multiplied by load factors to account for uncertainties and variability, used to determine the required strength in structural design.
A failure mode in steel connections where a block of material tears out along a combination of tension and shear planes under applied loads.
A layer of concrete applied atop filled or partially filled metal grid decks to protect against chlorides and enhance durability.
A material testing method performed on-site to measure the hardness of a structural component, often used to assess material properties without removing samples.
The seismic design force calculated for a structure based on its dynamic response modes, used to determine the scaling of element forces in earthquake-resistant design.
The portion of the total base shear acting on the superstructure immediately above the isolation plane, distinct from the shear across the isolators.
Transverse structural members that support the ribs and deck plate in an orthotropic steel deck, transferring loads to the main longitudinal girders.
The distance between points of lateral support in a structural member, affecting its stability and resistance to buckling.
A type of bracing that connects to a rigid structure and restrains lateral movement at specific points (nodes) in a structural system.
Coefficients used to allocate live loads to individual structural components based on approximate methods outlined in design specifications.
A type of brittle fracture in steel structures caused by high constraint conditions, such as closely spaced welds, which elevate stress concentrations and reduce material toughness.
An open-section steel beam with a distinctive 'I' shape, commonly used in bridge construction but offering lower torsional stiffness compared to closed-section alternatives.
The Strong-Column Weak-Beam ratio, a design criterion ensuring that columns are stronger than beams to promote ductile failure mechanisms in moment-resisting frames.
Coefficients applied to the nominal properties of an isolation system component to determine its upper and lower bound force-deflection behavior.
A structural element made of concrete poured on-site to distribute lateral forces and provide rigidity in a building's floor or roof system.
Methods used in structural engineering to analyze a building's response to earthquake ground motions over time, typically through dynamic analysis.
Deep foundation elements made of steel, concrete, or wood that are hammered or vibrated into the ground to support structures by transferring loads to deeper, more stable soil layers.
The design practice of limiting concrete cracking by specifying reinforcement spacing and size to ensure durability and serviceability under service loads.
A localized area in a structural wall where abrupt changes in geometry or stiffness occur, making it vulnerable to high shear stresses during lateral loading.
Reinforcement placed perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of a structural member to resist shear forces and improve ductility.
Graphical representations of earthquake ground motion showing structural response (e.g., acceleration) across a range of vibration periods.
Metallic or non-metallic substances intentionally added to steel to modify its properties, such as strength, hardness, or corrosion resistance.
The relative horizontal displacement between two consecutive floors of a building, often used as a measure of structural deformation under lateral loads.
A segmented portion of a larger diaphragm in a structure, designed to distribute lateral forces to the vertical elements of the lateral force-resisting system.
Longitudinal stiffening elements that reinforce the steel deck plate and span between transverse floorbeams in an orthotropic steel deck system.
A numerical value representing the live-load capacity of a bridge relative to a specific vehicle or load configuration.
A geometric property of a structural section that quantifies its resistance to warping deformation under torsional loads, negligible in closed-box sections like tub girders.
A form of material failure caused by the combined effects of tensile stress and a corrosive environment in susceptible metals like untempered steel.
Simplified structural analysis techniques used to estimate load distribution and structural responses without detailed computational modeling.
The deformation or stress in a girder flange caused by forces acting perpendicular to the plane of the web, often due to skew or curvature.
Structural steel connections that have been tested and approved in advance by a recognized authority, such as AISC, for use in specific applications without requiring project-specific testing.
The process of analyzing how the dynamic response of a structure is influenced by the interaction between its foundation and the underlying soil during seismic loading.
A structural element designed to resist lateral forces, such as wind or seismic loads, by transferring them to the foundation.
Structural components attached perpendicularly to the web of a girder to provide stability and resist out-of-plane distortion.
The total lateral force exerted at the base of a structure during seismic or wind events, calculated across the isolation plane or at the foundation level.
A device designed to detect seismic accelerations and trigger a shutdown of an elevator to prevent operation during or after an earthquake.
A phenomenon where the seismic response of a structure is reduced due to the spatial averaging of ground motion over the area of its foundation base slab.
The intersection of a beam and column in a structural frame, critical for transferring forces and ensuring stability under seismic loads.
Reinforcing elements, such as stirrups, designed to resist shear forces in a concrete beam.
A heat treatment process applied to steel to reduce brittleness, restore ductility, and adjust tensile strength to specified limits.
The capacity of a structural detail to withstand repeated stress cycles without developing cracks or failure over its service life.
The pressure exerted by a footing on the underlying soil, which must be distributed within allowable limits to prevent excessive settlement or loss of contact.
Three-dimensional graphical or analytical tools used to determine the effects of live loads on structural members by mapping load positions to force responses.
A coefficient used to adjust the strength calculations of structural members made from materials with differing yield strengths.
The depth at which a structure's foundation is placed below the ground surface, affecting the ground acceleration experienced by the structure.
A factor used to adjust the required shear strength of a diaphragm based on its design option and seismic demand level.
A type of braced frame where the centerlines of the braces, beams, and columns intersect at a single point to efficiently transfer lateral forces.
A structural design approach that evaluates performance against defined limit states, such as strength or serviceability, using partial safety factors.
A condition caused by the formation of nitrogen bubbles in the blood and tissues due to rapid ascent from depth, potentially resulting from exceeding no-decompression time limits.
A concrete placement process used to connect bridge girders to abutments or other structural elements, often after initial backfill or girder installation.
A ratio (2Dc/tw) used to assess the susceptibility of a web to buckling under compressive stresses in a cross-section.
The maximum moment a cross-section can resist when fully yielded, forming a plastic hinge under bending.
The initial tensile force applied to a bolt during assembly to improve joint performance under operational loads.
A component intended to fail under significant lateral loads, releasing the superstructure to allow activation of the isolation system.
A unique identifier assigned to a batch of steel during production, used for traceability of chemical composition and testing results.
A failure mode in structural elements under compressive stress where sudden lateral deflection or collapse occurs.
A factor applied to the nominal resistance of a structural element to account for uncertainties in material properties, dimensions, and construction quality.
Structural components that support the superstructure and allow controlled movement or rotation while transferring loads to the substructure.
Fatigue cracks that develop in structural details due to cyclic strains caused by out-of-plane movements or stiffness discontinuities.
A structural analysis method that evaluates the progressive deformation and failure of a system under incrementally applied loads, accounting for material and geometric nonlinearities.
A phenomenon in tension members where stress distribution is non-uniform due to uneven load transfer, accounted for by a reduction factor in strength calculations.
A specific set of factored loads applied simultaneously to a structure to evaluate its strength or stability under different conditions.
A graphical representation of seismic demand accounting for the nonlinear behavior of structures under earthquake loading, used to assess their capacity to absorb energy without failure.
A structural analysis method that models the entire bridge framing system as a series of beam elements, approximating deck stiffness and distributing loads through cross-frames.
Engineered devices or mechanisms integrated into structures to absorb and dissipate seismic energy, reducing structural damage during earthquakes.
Bridge deck systems where the entire depth of a metal grid is filled with concrete, often using precast panels or cast-in-place concrete for structural integrity.
A short structural member tested or analyzed to determine cross-sectional strength without considering length-dependent stability effects like buckling.
A specific load combination used in bridge design to evaluate serviceability conditions, such as slip resistance in connections, under normal operational loads.
The median (50th percentile) values of ground motion intensity measures, calculated as the antilogarithm of the average of logarithmic ground motion amplitudes.
An additional vertical load applied to a structure or soil, often from temporary or permanent loads like equipment or materials, that affects stability.
The number of stress cycles a structural detail can endure before failure occurs, as determined by its nominal stress range.
Low-cost components used in elevators to enhance their seismic performance by improving structural stability during an earthquake.
A shear stress induced in a structural member due to an applied torque or twisting moment.
Engineering structures, supports, or systems used during construction but not part of the permanent bridge.
A built-up structural member composed of three plates welded together, typically exhibiting higher fatigue resistance than cover-plated beams.
A structural section where concrete and steel components act together to resist loads, typically through shear connectors or bonding.
The bending moment in a bridge component induced during construction phases, such as erection or deck pouring, which must be considered in design.
A designation indicating that a steel product meets the requirements of two different grade specifications simultaneously.
Operating Basis Earthquake, a seismic event with a moderate level of ground motion used to evaluate structural performance under earthquake-induced loads.
A safety mechanism in elevators that activates to prevent the counterweight from derailing during seismic events.
A pier cap that is structurally connected or monolithic with the bridge girders, often used to distribute loads and improve structural continuity.
A failure mode in beams or girders where lateral displacement and twisting occur under bending loads due to insufficient restraint.
A weld of approximately triangular cross-section joining two surfaces at right angles, commonly used to attach stiffeners to a girder web.
Bridge deck systems where only a portion of the metal grid's depth is filled with concrete, reducing weight by omitting concrete in tension zones for simple span applications.
A multiplier applied to diaphragm shear reinforcement or connectors to ensure elastic shear response while allowing inelastic flexural behavior under seismic design objectives.
Submerged Arc Welding flux, a granular material used to shield the weld pool and arc from atmospheric contamination during welding.
A bridge deck system made of steel plates stiffened in orthogonal directions to efficiently distribute loads and reduce weight.
The anticipated maximum tensile capacity of a steel member or connection, calculated using material over-strength factors and nominal yield or ultimate strengths.
Gravity-Induced Lateral Demand, a design consideration accounting for additional lateral forces caused by vertical irregularities such as sloping columns or uneven story heights.
The Maximum Considered Earthquake ground motion, representing a more severe seismic event than the DE, used to assess structural resilience and performance limits.

Abutment structures that partially integrate with the bridge deck, typically allowing some movement while still reducing expansion joint use and distributing loads between the superstructure and substructure.
The lateral curvature or deviation from a straight line in a precast concrete girder, affecting its stability during erection.
The ratio of the elastic modulus of steel to the elastic modulus of concrete, used to transform steel area into an equivalent concrete area for stress analysis.
Deep foundation elements used to transfer structural loads to deeper, more stable soil or rock layers, particularly under lateral loading conditions.
SMAW electrodes with a coating designed to limit moisture absorption, ensuring minimal hydrogen content in the resulting weld metal.
A specific design load combination in bridge engineering that includes factored permanent and live loads to evaluate structural strength under ultimate limit states.
Transverse reinforcement designed to restrain the lateral expansion of core concrete under compressive loads, enhancing its strength and ductility.
A method of bridge construction where spans are built sequentially, with piles for the next bent driven from the completed span to minimize environmental impact.
The separation or splitting of layers within a composite material, such as FRP, often due to stress or degradation.
A geometric property of a cross-section that determines its resistance to bending or flexural deformation, critical for stiffener design.
The line in a beam's cross-section where the longitudinal stress and strain are zero under bending.
The specified minimum thickness of concrete between the surface of the slab and the reinforcement to protect it from corrosion and ensure structural integrity.
The torsional rigidity of a beam section, contributing to its resistance against twisting and providing additional restraint in buckling analysis.
The threshold value of the web slenderness parameter below which a web can achieve its full plastic moment without local buckling.
The gap between the edge of a hole and the edge of a structural member or between the edges of adjacent holes.
Horizontal displacement of soil layers, typically occurring on gentle slopes or near water bodies during earthquakes, leading to ground failure.
The predicted tensile capacity of a steel member or connection at fracture, based on the ultimate tensile strength and material-specific adjustment factors.
A type of weld made in a pre-prepared groove between two workpieces, such as flange and web butt joints in bridges.
Steel plates attached to the bottom flange of a beam to distribute bearing reactions and provide a level surface for bearings, often beveled to correct girder misalignment.
Multipliers applied to nominal loads to ensure safety and reliability by accounting for potential deviations in load magnitude or application.
A design parameter for fire protection sprinkler systems, derived from the mapped short-period response parameter (Ss), used to calculate lateral forces.
The area close to an earthquake fault where ground motions exhibit distinct characteristics, such as directivity pulses and high velocity.
A redundancy within a primary member cross-section where fracture of one component does not propagate through the entire member, remains detectable by inspection, and prevents bridge collapse.
The calculated movements between different parts of a structure caused by seismic forces, used to design connections and joints.
A structural wall made of precast concrete designed to resist lateral forces, particularly seismic loads, in a building.
The gradual deformation or displacement of bearing pads under sustained loads, influencing the stability and alignment of bridge girders.
A reinforced concrete diaphragm designed to yield primarily through flexural deformation, allowing the use of a higher force reduction factor (Rs).
A structural failure mode where beams undergo plastic deformation (yielding) under seismic or extreme loads, redistributing forces within the frame.
A method for combining modal responses in seismic analysis to account for correlation between closely spaced modes of vibration.
A qualitative scale used to measure the effects of earthquakes on people, structures, and the Earth's surface, often correlated with quantitative ground motion data.
The difference between the maximum and minimum applied stresses during cyclic loading, identified as the primary parameter governing fatigue crack growth in welded structures.
Thresholds based on parameters like frequency ratio and mass ratio that determine whether a secondary component can be analyzed independently of the primary structure in seismic design.
The curve defining the interior (lower) surface of an arch, also referred to as the soffit.
The minimum required compressive strength of concrete, as designated in design documents, used to determine structural performance and capacity.
Structural components in a bridge whose failure would likely result in collapse, requiring higher toughness steel and stricter fabrication controls.
A bracing system, such as a lateral truss, that restrains the movement of a braced point in relation to adjacent braced points in a structure.
Temporary structures used to support a permanent structure during its construction or repair.
A type of torsional resistance in a structural member where the cross-section does not remain plane, resulting in axial stresses and non-uniform twist.
Uncertainty in seismic hazard analysis arising from incomplete knowledge or alternative models, often addressed using logic trees to weigh different scenarios.
Bends at the ends of reinforcing bars, such as stirrups or ties, designed to anchor the bar within concrete and prevent pull-out under load.
A mechanically stabilized earth retaining wall system used to support soil laterally and integrate with abutment structures.
A diaphragm design approach that aims to maintain the diaphragm's elastic behavior during the Maximum Considered Earthquake (MCE).
Reinforced structural walls surrounding elevator shafts that provide lateral stability and support to the building.
The maximum load-carrying capacity of a structural cross-section when it is entirely yielded and forms a plastic hinge under combined axial force and bending moment.
Vertical vessels or tanks supported by a cylindrical shell (skirt) at their base, transferring loads to the foundation.
Lateral walls connected to abutments, often designed as cantilevers or supported by foundations, to retain soil and transfer loads, sometimes analyzed using plate theory.
